div.p: In this paper, we present algorithm BandWidth Inheritance ( B W I ) , a new scheduling strategy that extends the bandwidth reservation approach to systems where tasks can interact through shared resources. T h e proposed algorithm provides temporal isolation between independent groups of tasks, and enables a schedulability analysis for guaranteeing the performance of realtime tasks. After showing that B W I is the natural extension of the well-known Priority Inheritance Protocol to dynamic reservation. systems, a formal analysis of the algorithm is presented, and simple guarantee tests for hard real-time tasks are proposed.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: An Open System is a general purpose computer systern in which it is not possible to know a-priori how many applications need to be executed and the characteristics thereof. Typically, in an Open System applications with different levels of Quality of Service may coexists: hard real-time, multi-media and interactive non-real-time applications.

The Open System concept was originally presented in [9], where a dedicated aperiodic server is used t o serve each different application, and a custom scheduler can be associated to each application in a hierarchical way. However, the algorithms proposed in [9] require a-priori knowledge of the tasks' execution times even for soft real-time tasks and this can be restrictive for a real Open System.

A better approach is to provide isolation between applications, such that an application is protected from the misbehaviors of the other applications. This property is called Bandwidth Isolation (BIP) [2, 111: the net effect is that each application executes as it were on a slower dedicated processor. Based on this approach, Giuseppe Lipari, Luca Abeni Scuola Superiore S.Anna { lipari,luca}@sssup.it the Resource Reservation framework [15, 181 has been proven very effective in the joint scheduling of Hard Real Time (HRT) and Soft Real Time (SRT) applications in Open Systems. In this framework, when an application arrives in the system requiring a certain level of QoS, an admission test is run: if, given the actual system load, the required level of QoS can be guaranteed] the application is accepted in the system and assigned a certain fraction of the system resources. Many scheduling algorithms based on the Resource Reservation Framework have been proposed. The ternporal isolation and Resource Reservation concepts were first introduced in RT-Mach [15], and evolved in the Resource Kernel [U]. A Resource Kernel (RK) permits to reserve hardware resources t o applications, guaranteeing that each application can use a resource for a tirne C each period T . The RK technology is particularly interesting, since it seamlessly provides QoS even to non real-time legacy applications, and has been recently ported to Linux [17].

Resource Reservation techniques, originally based on a fixed priorities assignment, have also been applied to dynamic priority schemes [7, 21. One of the advantages of using dynamic priorities (and in particular an EDF scheduler), is t o improve the usage of the available resources. The Constant Bandwidth Server (CBS) [211 uses a deadline postponing mechanism to efficiently provide bandwidth isolation. In particular, the CBS algorithm provides real-time guarantees to hard real-time tasks and probabilistic guarantees t o soft real-time tasks. Recently, some reclaiming mechanisms [13, 51 have been added to the CBS.

However, all the algorithms presented so far support only independent tasks: a task is not allowed to block or suspend itself, otherwise certain properties, such as the BIP, cannot be guaranteed. This is a major limitation for their implementation in a real operating system: in the real world, many real-time applications communicate by means of shared memory and access mutually exclusive resource.

In the real-time system literature a great amount of work has been addressed to the problem of providing guarantees to hard real-time tasks accessing mutually exclusive resources. In fact, if classical mutex semaphores are used, a particular problem arises, usually referred as the priority inversion problem. This problem was first described by Sha, Rajkumar and Lehoczky in [19]: if a higher priority task is blocked on a semaphore by a lower priority task, and another medium priority task arrives, the latter can preempt the lower priority task causing an unbounded blocking delay to the higher priority task. In the same paper, the authors proposed two algorithms to overcome this problem, the Priority Inheritance and the Priority Ceiling protocols. Almost at the same time, another protocol similar to Priority Ceiling, the Stack Resource Policy, was presented by Baker in [3].

In [lo], it is shown how to combine the SRP algorithm with aperiodic servers, in order to share resources between aperiodic tasks and hard real-time tasks. This approach has been recently applied to the CBS in [6]. However, this kind of solutions require an apriori knowledge of the maximum resource usage time for each task, and in an open system it is impossible t o have such an a-priori knowledge.

For this reason, resource sharing protocols such as PI, PC, or SRP cannot be directly used in an Open Systern. For example, the CBS algorithm assumes a very simple task model (the Liu and Layland task model [14]), where no task can suspend itself or block on a critical section. If tasks are allowed to suspend, inconsistencies can arise in the CBS algorithm. In [8], similar problems have been investigated in the context of a reservation based system such as the RK; in particular, the inheritance and ceiling techniques have been modified to correctly work in a reservation system, and one of the proposed solutions (namely, the Reserve Inheritance approach) results t o be similar to the one presented in this paper.

div.head: System Model
div.p: A real-time task ri is a stream of jobs, or instances, J,,j; each job is a request for execution on a shared processor, and is characterized by an arrival time a i j , an execution time ci,j and an absolute deadline di,j. A real-time task is also assigned a relative deadline Di, and d i j = ai,j + Di.

Real-time tasks can be hard or soft: a task ri is said to be a hard real-time task (HRT) if all its jobs must complete within their deadline otherwise a critical failure may occur in the system. Every HRT task ri is characterized by a Minimum Interarrival Time T i = minj{ai,j+lai,j} and a Worst Case Execution Time (WCET) Ci = maxj{ci,j}.

A task is said to be a soft real-time task (SRT) if In this paper, we propose t o schedule each task through a dedicated seruer. A server is a "scheduling entity", characterized by a scheduling priority, that is inserted in the system ready queue. Each task is associated to a server, and when the server is selected by the scheduler, the associated task is dispatched. For the sake of simplicity, in the remaining of the paper we will write "server Si is blocked", meaning that the task served by S i is blocked, and "Si is executing'' meaning that the task served by Si is executing.

Each server is characterized by two parameters Qi and Pi, with the meaning that each task is allowed to execute &i every Pi units of time. The fraction Ui = represents the share of the processor reserved to server Si. Our attention is restricted to systems where all servers execute on a single shared processor and the sum of the processor shares of all the servers is no more than one: xi QilPi 5 1.

div.head: Requirements.
div.p: In order t o be successfully used in an open system, the scheduling discipline must not require any a-priori information about the tasks' execution patterns. In particular: 0 The scheduling algorithm has no a priori knowledge of which resources a task will access; it can only be known on line when the task tries to lock a resource. Nor do we require any a priori upper bound on the duration [i,j of a critical section.

Note that these requirements do not exclude the pos- sibility to perform a schedulability analysis on a subset of HRT tasks. If the application designer performs an accurate timing analysis on each HRT task and is able to bound the execution times and the duration of the critical sections, then it is possible to find an assignment of parameters t o the servers which guarantees the schedulability of the HRT tasks. The isolation property ensures that, even if SRT tasks are present in the system together with HRT tasks, the schedulability of the HRT tasks will not be jeopardized.

div.head: Sharing resources with CBS
div.p: Using the CBS algorithm, if tasks access critical section through classical semaphores, problems can arise.
As an example, suppose that server Si is blocked on a shared resource by server S j , which has a greater deadline.

The blocked server S, must wait for the low priority server S, holding the resource; in the meanwhile, inany medium priority server can execute, further delaying S,. This is a form of priority inversion, and can be partially solved by introducing the Priority Inheritance Protocol (PIP) among the servers. The PIP is briefly presented in Section 4.

In the admission test, blocking times are not accounted for: then, it is possible that some server S h , which does not access any critical section, misses its deadline even if its served task is requiring exactly what it has declared. This is a failure of the bandwidth isolation property: in fact, r h is independent from ra and rJ.

in order to provide a guarantees fot HRT tasks, we must account for the blocking time experienced by a server. There are different ways to account for this blocking time: in Section 4.1 we will analyze the different possibilities.

A first trivial solution, which maintains the CBS properties, is to consider a job that resumes from a blocked status as a new instance of the task. Therefore, when a job is "un-blocked" , the corresponding server is assigned a new pair budgetldeadline, according to the CBS rule.

This method is simple and effective for scheduling SRT tasks and guarantees the bandwidth isolation property among servers. However, it is not suitable for HRT tasks. In fact, it is difficult to bound the completion time of a task because we cannot know a-priori when the task will be un-blocked and which scheduling deadline will be assigned to its server.

div.head: The Priority Inheritance Protocol
div.p: The Priority Inheritance Protocol (PIP) was first presented in [19] t o solve the priority inversion problem. It is based on the following rules: when an higher priority job JH wants t o access a critical section and it is blocked on it, the low priority job JL which holds the lock on the resource inherits the priority of J H .
when JL unlocks the resource, it returns to the priority it had at the time it acquired the lock.
Notice that, if more than one higher priority task is blocked on the critical section, it is possible for J L to inherit more than one priority (multiple inheritance).

Even though the PIP was thought in the context of fixed priority scheduling, it can be applied also in the context of dynamic priority scheduling, and the same basic properties hold: Using these properties, it is possible to give a sufficient condition for the schedulability of a set of n HRT periodic tasks. Suppose that the task are ordered by non decreasing periods (Ti < Tj + i < j ) . The schedulability condition is the following:

where C, and Tj are respectively the worst case execution time and the period of task rJ and B, is the worst case blocking time experienced by task 7%. There are two kinds of blocking times that contribute to B,:
direct blockingwhen a job JH tries to access a resource R which is already locked by a lower priority job.
push-trough blockingwhen a j o b J is blocked because a lower priority job JL has inherited a priority higher than J .

The Priority Inheritance Protocol reduces the blocking delay of high priority jobs but has several limitations: first, it does not prevent deadlock; second, it causes the problem of chuined blocking where a job can be blocked once for each critical section it tries to access. Thus, even if the blocking time is reduced, it can still be quite high. To overcome these limitations, in [19] Sha, Lehozcy and Rajkumar propose the Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP) which prevents deadlock and chained blocking.

However, in order to use ceiling protocols like PCP or SRP, the system must know in advance which resources a task will access. This can be done only at system start-up or before a task begins the execution of the first instance. For this reason, the PCP cannot directly be used in an Open System. In the remaining of the paper, we will use the basic Priority Inheritance protocol.

div.head: Using the Priority Inheritance Protocol with the CBS
div.p: The simple introduction of the PIP on top of the CBS mechanism raises two questions: 0 how to account for the blocking time of a task? 0 what happens if some task requires more than declared?

A first solution would be t o account for this blocking time in the admission test: where Bi represents the maximum blocking time experienced by each server. Again, this solution is not suitable for an open system. In fact, in order to compute the maximum blocking time of each server, even SRT tasks must declare the maximum duration of the critical sections on each accessed resource, and this is in contrast with the goal of a scheduler which is independent from the actual requirements of the tasks.

In addition, if a SRT task fails to respect its requirements, and holds a critical section for longer than declared, some server will miss its deadline and, since we are using an EDF scheduler, we cannot know in advance which server is going to fail.

Finally, there is yet another question concerning SRT tasks that need t o be answered. In the origi-nal CBS formulation, when the budget of a server is exhausted, the server deadline is postponed and the server budget is immediately recharged. What happens if a server exhausts its budget while it is in a critical section and it has inherited the deadline of some other server? Which deadline has t o be postponed, the server original deadline or the inherited deadline? How much should the capacity be recharged?

To answer all these questions, we shall follow a different approach. In the next section, we will fuse the PIP and the CBS in a single algorithm called Bandwidth Inheritance (BWI) protocol. The basic idea is that when a lower priority server blocks a higher priority server, it inherits the pair (q, S) of the blocked server.

div.head: Interference Time Computation
div.p: In the general case, an exact computation of I, is a complex problem. At first glance, the problem is similar to the computation of the blocking times B, for the PIP. However, when considering algorithm BWI the problem is slightly different. For example, with BWI there is no push-through blocking; in addition, a server can decrease its priority by postponing its deadline while in a critical section. The problem becomes more difficult when tasks are allowed to nest critical sections.

In [16], Rajkumar proved that, when using the basic Priority Inheritance Protocol, the problem of computing the blocking time of a task in the general case (allowing nested critical sections) is NP hard. We claim that the complexity of computing the interference time in the general case is also NP hard. For this reason, we will also consider a simpler case without nested critical sections, for which it is simpler to perform an exact analysis.

In the following, we will present two algorithms for computing the interference time of a task. First, we will consider the general case (with nested critical sections), and we will show that if no deadline in a partition is postponed, then an upper bound to the interference time is given by the same algorithm used for the computation of the blocking time in the basic Priority Inheritance Protocol. Hence, if all tasks in a partition are hard tasks, the classical Priority Inheritance analysis can be used (at the cost of an over-pessimistic admission test).

Second, we will consider the case in which critical sections cannot be nested, and we will develop a more precise analysis. As a result, we will present a more accurate algorithm for the computation of the interference time for a task, and we will explicitly consider interactions between soft and hard tasks.
Before proceeding we need to introduce some preliminary results that will be used in the following analysis.

div.head: Nested Critical Sections
div.p: In this subsection, we will analyze the general case in which critical sections can be nested. Since the analysis is very complex, we are going t o re-use some important results from the classical Priority Inheritance analysis. In order to do that, we need to suppose that all tasks inside a partition are HRT tasks. In this case, the following lemma helps us:

Lemma 4 Under the hypothesis that the deadlines of all the servers in ri are neverpostponed, task ri, served by server S i with budget Qi and period Pi, can be blocked only by tasks served by servers having longer periods (like in fixed priority systems).

Looking at Lemma 2, Lemma 3, and Lemma 4, we can see that they are equivalent to the PIP properties proved in [19]. Hence, the interference time Ii can be computed as the blocking time for the basic PIP case. Algorithms for computing such a blocking time have been proposed in [16] and [4].

Hence, in order not t o miss any deadline in ri it is sufficient to compute the interference times using one of those algorithms, and to assign Q j = Cj + Ij to each task rj E I'i, according t o Theorem 4.

div.p: As an example, consider a HRT task and a SRT task which access the same shared Iesource through a common shared library. If the critical sections are implemented as library functions whose execution time can be bounded, then we can still be able to compute the interference time that the soft task "steals" to the hard task. Indeed, this is a common case in a real operating system.

For this reason, it can be desirable to guarantee a single HRT task T~ even in the case in which there are SRT tasks in its partition. In this case, the bandwidth assigned to the SRT tasks does not influence the behavior of the HRT task, and can be allocated based on the average case. However, the server for the HRT task must always be assigned a budget and a period based on the worst case.

In this case, Lemma 2 and Lemma 3 are still valid, but Lemma 4 is not. As an example. conside1 a SRT task r, that is served by a server S, with a period P3 < P,. However, if r., executes for more than declared, it can deplete the server budget and postpone its deadline, decreasing its dynamic priority. In this case, it can later be preempted by S, while inside a critical section, and block r,, contributing to its interference time I,.

Hence, when considering SRT tasks in the same partition of a HRT task r,, the algorithm for computing I, must consider u11 the tasks that are sharing resources with -ra and not only those with longer periods. The results presented in this section section are valid for partitions in which tasks do not use nested critical sections. If, instead, nested critical sections are present in the partition, only the temporal isolation (Theorem 3) and hard schedulability (Theorem 4) properties are verified. In this case, the interference times must be computed as the blocking times in the priority inheritance case. However, as shown, this condition is not tight. We are currently developing a new algorithm for computing 1, in the case of nested critical sections.

div.head: Conclusions and future work
div.p: In this paper, we presented the Bandwidth Inheritance Protocol, a novel scheduling discipline that permits t o share resources between applications in an open system. Coherently with the Resource Reservation approach, the BWI protocol provides some temporal isolation properties without requiring any a-priori knowledge about the the structure and on the temporal behavior of the tasks.

In addition, a schedulability analysis for HRT tasks has been developed and presented in this paper. This analysis is based on the most important formal properties of the BWI algorithm, that are presented and proved in the paper.

As explained in Section 6 , we are still working on a moxe accurate schedulability analysis for the general case considering nested critical sections. Moreover, we are planning t o develop a probabilistic analysis for SRT tasks.

For what concerns the algorithm, we are currently analyzing better strategies for coping with "misbehaved" tasks that use the shared resource more that the declared < time. Roughly speaking, these tasks can L'steal'l CPU bandwidth t o the other tasks belonging to their partition r,, compromising their guarantee. We are currently testing different mechanisms and policies that can reduce (but not eliminate) this effect, in order to penalize the misbehaved tasks inside a partition.
